text_read: full text of Ch. 11 Trataka, Ch. 14 Chidakasha and Ch. 15 Ajna Chakra Dharana; Ch. 19 Vyoma Panchaka skimmed for light passages (Opus, from the user's PDF)
mode_evidence: Two modes are worked deliberately. The bahya-antar trataka begins with a perceptual afterimage ('a tiny, luminous, coloured dot' seen in chidakasha, its colour changing with gazing time) and, when it vanishes, asks the practitioner to 'recollect' it, so the later rounds shade into willed recall; the aim is an inner image as vivid as the outer object ('dharana' as seeing, versus 'kalpana', merely thinking). Open-eye practices are plainly perceptual: a silver, hazy shadow seen against the sky after shadow-gazing; 'visions start floating' in total darkness; visions come in the crystal 'even while your eyes are open'. Chidakasha stage 7 is perceptual (spontaneous streaks, points and clusters of light, which the book also calls an optical effect in the brain). Vyoma Panchaka lights are willed visualization; the text itself calls the ring of light 'a voluntary vision'.
onset_evidence: Explicit induction for those who cannot hold an inner image: combined outer-inner trataka 'is useful for people who are not able to develop an inner image at will'; inner trataka alone is reserved for those who already can, and trying it with a vague or absent image ends in sleep or wandering thought. Time scales: a round begins at about five minutes (three minutes outer gazing) and grows to half an hour (three minutes outer, twenty-seven inner); eleven rounds make one dharana; the Sri Yantra sequence is built up week by week. Says even beginners will have experiences after a short period. Shoonya drishti 'takes a long time'. Darkness-gazing is reserved for those with a disciplined inner life. No grace or transmission requirement is stated.

conditions.posture: steadiest possible seated posture, siddhasana or padmasana preferred; kaya sthairyam (total body stillness) first
conditions.gaze_or_eye_position: no blinking or eye movement; eyes relaxed, not straining; nose-tip and eyebrow-centre convergence (agochari, shambhavi) as outer trataka; counter-image held at the eyebrow centre
conditions.setting: candle: no other light, no breeze, flame at eye level an arm's length away; black dot: good light from behind; crystal: dim light on a black cloth; darkness: total darkness; shadow: sun at the back, then the sky
conditions.duration_and_schedule: 3 to 5 minutes outer gazing (crystal up to 10); inner phase up to 27 minutes per round; eleven rounds to one dharana; best 4 to 6 a.m. on an empty stomach, or late at night before meditation
conditions.prerequisites: antar trataka requires a clear inner image; shoonya drishti only after antar trataka is mastered; darkness trataka only for the mentally stable
conditions.other: close the eyes before tears fall in the raja-yoga form (tears belong to the hatha-yoga cleansing form); palming at the end; no glasses

stages.label: bahir trataka
stages.description: outer gazing at a steady object without blinking

stages.label: bahya-antar trataka
stages.description: afterimage at the eyebrow centre: a luminous coloured dot that fades, vanishes and returns in new colours until it merges into the dark background

stages.label: dharana
stages.description: after eleven rounds the inner image is 'absolutely clear', the candle seen in every detail with eyes closed

stages.label: dhyana
stages.description: the inner object acquires three dimensions and is as real as external sight

stages.label: shoonya drishti
stages.description: open-eyed gazing at nothing until the eyes dim and nothing is seen

what_to_do_with_light: Hold the counter-image steadily at the eyebrow centre; follow it gently back if it drifts; when it vanishes keep the eyes closed and gather it again; with spontaneous chidakasha lights, watch without analysing and identify the colours; with visions in darkness, stay aware but uninvolved.
obstacles_and_fixes: image unclear: be aware of whatever can be seen; relax the eye muscles
image drifts: follow it and bring it back to the eyebrow centre
image fades: keep the eyes closed and recreate it
eye strain: breathe to and from ajna through the eyebrow centre; rest the eyes
double object: change the dot size
cautions: never gaze directly at the sun (use its reflection in still water or a pea-sized hole in dark cloth, as the book also prescribes); direct moon-gazing can unbalance the mind
darkness trataka raises subconscious fears as visions and is not for the restless or unstable
in mirror or water gazing, whatever appears is one's own projection; leave the practice if psychic apparitions emerge
do not strain the eyes; trataka is heat-producing
interpretation: Trataka stabilises the retinal image until perception blanks out, isolating the nervous system ('sushumna awakening'); the inner screen (chidakasha) shows impressions from deeper consciousness, and the clear inner image marks dharana proper.
practice_summary: Sit motionless. Gaze at a candle flame at eye level, an arm's length away, without blinking, for three minutes. Close the eyes and look at the afterimage at the eyebrow centre: a small luminous dot whose colour depends on how long you gazed. Watch it steadily; if it drifts, bring it back; when it fades, keep the eyes closed and gather it again until it finally merges into the dark. That is one round. Extend the inner phase until a round lasts half an hour; eleven rounds 'make one dharana', when the candle can be seen in full detail with the eyes closed. The same method works with a black dot, a flower (whose afterimage is first a disc of the opposite colour), a deity picture framed in black, or the Sri Yantra built up week by week. Open-eye variants: gaze at your shadow, then up at the sky to see its silver image; gaze into total darkness or into a crystal until visions come.

key_passages.anchor: The method of outer and inner trataka combined is useful for people who are not able to develop an inner image at will
key_passages.paraphrase: Combined outer and inner trataka is for people who cannot produce an inner image at will; inner trataka alone is for those who already can, and trying it without a clear image leads to sleep or drifting thought.

key_passages.locator: Ch. 11, Trataka Two (Bahya-Antar Drishti), Technique 1: candle flame
key_passages.anchor: See somewhere in chidakasha a tiny, luminous, coloured dot
key_passages.paraphrase: After three minutes of gazing, the afterimage is seen in chidakasha as a tiny luminous dot whose colour depends on gazing time (black, white or dull brown after a minute; bright red after about five); it fades, vanishes and returns in another colour until it merges into the background.

key_passages.anchor: Eleven rounds of trataka make one dharana, which means that the mental image becomes absolutely clear
key_passages.paraphrase: Rounds lengthen from five minutes to half an hour; eleven rounds make one dharana, when the image is absolutely clear. Seeing the object is dharana; merely thinking of it is kalpana.

key_passages.locator: Ch. 11, Trataka Two, Technique 8: chhaya upasana
key_passages.anchor: you will perceive a great shadow cast over the background of the sky
key_passages.paraphrase: After gazing at the throat point of one's shadow, looking up shows a great silver, hazy shadow on the sky; repeated, it takes on the form of one's own shadow.

key_passages.locator: Ch. 11, Trataka Four (Shoonya Drishti), Technique 4: darkness
key_passages.anchor: After some time the darkness vanishes and visions start floating
key_passages.paraphrase: Gazing open-eyed into total darkness, the darkness gives way to floating visions, said to bring up subconscious fears; reserved for those with mental control and a disciplined inner life.

key_passages.anchor: Sometimes a cluster of light or colour manifests in chidakasha and remains there for a few moments
key_passages.paraphrase: With eyes closed, watch the spontaneous streaks, points, shades and clusters of light and colour on the inner screen without analysing them; earlier the book trains the practitioner to identify each colour as it appears.
